items.text: SEASON 11 · EPISODE 8 · DRAFT  The Brennock County EOC · between storms · Maya, Wendell (county IT), the state’s flood-model contractor and Director Oduya · Level L6 · Mastery support (reference only — choose the tool and say why)  The room needs partners — the state, the utility, contractors with better models than the county can afford. One of them just plugged into the operations network to save eight minutes.  ⚑ RV-182: the network is Wendell’s; access and review are county IT security’s; a partner’s laptop is his own. Governance only. RV-183: figures illustrative. Some choices run on a clock — and some depend on your loadout.

items.title: The Unknown Laptop
items.stakes: A contractor's laptop is on the operations network, because the right way to share a file was eight minutes slower.
items.reward: Partners with a network of their own — and an operations network that lets nothing unknown in.

objectives.text: Decide how the file gets there
Decide what stops the next cable

items.rumor: Make the right path the easy one.

items.prompt: 14:10. A state contractor's laptop is on the operations network at the UTILITY desk. What do you do?

hints.text: What's the fastest move that's yours — and who owns the rest?

options.label: Leave it — he's from the state
options.result: It stays connected all afternoon, trying the GIS server's shares.
options.consequence: A badge isn't a network policy.

options.label: Ask him, politely, to unplug now; note the desk, the port and the time; call Wendell
options.result: He unplugs, embarrassed: “I just needed to share a file.” Port 3B-17, 14:06–14:10. Wendell's on it.
options.consequence: Fast, polite, recorded — and the owner told.

options.label: Pull the uplink for that whole row of desks
options.result: Wendell: “My switch — and you'd take four agencies off with him.”
options.fail: The switch is the network owner's.

options.label: Take the laptop off the desk
options.result: Wendell: “It's his. Security decides anything more.”
options.consequence: Seizing someone else's device isn't yours.
options.fail: A partner's device is his; any review is security's.

items.title: Thirty-eight of sixty-four.
items.body: Wendell walks the desks with Maya and his port list. Thirty-eight of the room's sixty-four desk ports are live on the operations network, and nothing checks what's plugged into them. ‘Spare (live)’, the list says, twenty-four times. The contractor didn't break in. He found an open door that had been open for years.
items.label: Test: how many doors — and who reviews what came through?

items.title: 3B-17 · ‘spare (live)’
items.body: Wendell's switch port list: ‘3B-17 — spare (live).’ Twenty-four ports carry the same note. Nobody had ever needed to switch a spare off — until one was used.

items.title: One program, six thousand machines
items.body: In November 1988 a self-copying program released onto the early internet spread from computer to computer in hours, slowing or stopping thousands of university and government machines. Nobody had imagined that a network of trusted colleagues needed doors that closed. Within weeks the first computer emergency response team was set up — to coordinate the answer the next time.

items.title: Eight minutes.
items.body: Why plug in? The contractor is honest: the partner Wi-Fi is slow, and the GIS desk needed the model before the briefing. Maya works it out with him. Three gigabytes over the 50 Mb/s partner link, through the county's scanned transfer service: 480 seconds. Eight minutes. He'd saved about seven and a half — and put an unknown laptop on the network every agency depends on. The switch log shows it tried the GIS server's shares while it was there; the security officer takes it from there.
items.label: Test: what did he actually save?

items.prompt: He still needs the 3 GB model on the GIS desk before 17:00. How?
unknown: Whether he knows the transfer service exists
items.risk: The GIS desk without the model — or the door reopened.
timeout: The contractor plugs back in ‘just for a minute’.

hints.text: What's the right path — and how long does it really take?

options.label: A USB stick to the GIS desk
options.result: Unknown media, straight into a county machine.
options.consequence: The same door, in a smaller box.

options.label: The partner network and the county's scanned file-transfer service — he uploads, GIS pulls it
options.result: Eight minutes. GIS has it by 14:25; the contractor asks for the link to use next time.
options.consequence: The right path, shown to be easy.

options.label: Plug back in, just for two minutes
options.result: Two minutes of the same problem.

unknown: Who else has plugged in before
items.risk: The next unknown device, on a busier day.

hints.text: What would make the right path easy and the wrong one impossible — and noticed?

items.note: Draft decision (DR-S11E08). Option B needs Monitoring & tools at LIMITED or better.

options.label: Glue the spare ports shut
options.result: The next agency that needs a port gets a screwdriver.
options.consequence: A physical hack instead of a design.

options.label: Wendell switches off unused ports and turns on port security; marked PARTNER jacks at every desk on an internet-only network; a network card at visitor check-in; an alert on any new device on the operations network
options.result: Done by Thursday. A test laptop on a desk port goes nowhere, and Wendell's phone buzzes in four seconds.
options.consequence: Doors closed by their owner, an easy right path, and an alarm on the rest.

options.label: Switch off the unused ports and put a sign at every desk
options.result: Most doors closed. Nobody knows when someone tries one.
options.consequence: The best you can do without monitoring — closed, but unwatched.

options.label: Ban partner laptops from the room
options.result: The state's modeller works from the car park. The model arrives late.
options.consequence: Keeps out the people the room needs.

items.text: ✦ UX RULE #109 · AVERY'S LENS  Partners get a network — just not the operations one  Visitors and partner agencies need to work in the room. Give them their own network and a scanned way to share files, so nobody plugs into the operations network to save eight minutes.  A contractor plugged into a spare cable to share a flood model, because the right way was eight minutes slower — and 38 of 64 desk ports would have let anyone do the same.

items.alt: The port map after Thursday: 14 green squares for county equipment, 12 blue PARTNER jacks on an internet-only network, and the rest grey, switched off; a new device on any port gets no network and raises an alert.
items.caption: Doors that close.

items.prompt: I should have switched those ports off years ago.

options.label: “You've been running a whole county's network with a team of two. Now you've got the evidence to ask for the time.”
options.reply: And the director signs the visitor card. I like that.

options.label: “Nobody thinks about ports.”
options.reply: I do. I just never had the afternoon.

items.alt: The EOC; Wendell holds a new port map; Director Oduya holds a visitor card with a network section.

bubbles.text: Test laptop on a desk port: nothing. My phone buzzed in four seconds.
And every visitor gets this card at the door. Partner jacks are blue.

items.title: name · agency · time
items.body: The EOC's visitor sheet: name, agency, time in, time out. Nothing about devices, networks or where to plug in. The contractor had signed it at 13:58.

items.alt: The EOC in a quiet afternoon; Director Oduya points at a long list of findings pinned beside the wall; Maya reads it.

bubbles.text: Eleven findings from two storms. A state grant that covers maybe half. Which half?
The half that fails worst. And we write down the rest.

items.text: FIELD NOTE —  Every live port is a door onto the operations network. Switch off the unused ones, check the used ones, alert on anything new — through the network’s owner. Give partners an easier right path: marked partner jacks, an internet-only network and a scanned file-transfer service (t = S ÷ r shows what shortcuts really save). Ask, record and call the owner; never seize someone else’s device.
